targets.authors: Gerber, Alan S., and Donald P. Green.
targets.title: The Effects of Personal Canvassing, Telephone Calls, and Direct Mail on Voter Turnout: A Field Experiment.
targets.evidence_quote: Returning to the original data files, we reconstructed both the household-level and the individual-level New Haven study for purposes of preparing this correction.
targets.outcome_computational_quote: Looking first at the model without covariates, we see that the estimated effect of face-to-face canvassing changes from 8.7 (published) to 8.4 (corrected). Mail’s effect changes from 0.58 (published) to 0.51 (corrected). The coefficient estimate for phone calls remains negative. The published value of −4.7 is corrected to be −1.9.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: Correcting the coding errors in the New Haven study changes none of the substantive conclusions that flow from it.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Reconstructing and correcting original data changes the reported coefficients beyond rounding (notably the telephone estimate), while the authors explicitly find the substantive conclusions unchanged under corrections and sample/model variations. New 2002 sample evidence separately confirms the original null telephone result; it is not used to decide the robustness axis.

targets.title: Do Get-Out-the-Vote Calls Reduce Turnout? The Importance of Statistical Methods for Field Experiments.
targets.evidence_quote: Replication of Professor Imai’s (2005) analysis reveals a series of errors that call into question the magnitude, significance, and robustness of his matching estimates.
targets.outcome_computational_quote: Table 9 of Imai 2005 exaggerates the significance of the phone effect by reporting a coefficient of 6.5 with a standard error of 3.2. These numbers imply a t-ratio of 2.03, which tells the reader at a glance that the effect is statistically significant using a two-sided test (p < .05). When these numbers are replicated using 500,000 bootstrap samples rather than 500, the correct estimate is 6.2, with a t-ratio of 1.87 (see Table 2).
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: The estimated effects of phone calls fall to insignificance when based on the actual sample. His matching program generates an estimate of 5.1 (SE = 3.3) when performing one-to-five matching on the actual sample, and this number drops to 3.6 (SE = 4.5) when one-to-five matching is performed with replacement.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Re-running the original matching analysis yields substantive numerical discrepancies and inflated reported significance. Alternative matching specifications and analysis of actual rather than bootstrap samples remove significance. This target is itself an earlier reanalysis, directly re-tested here.

reasoning: Primary article verified by title, authors, journal pages 301–313, and complete reference list. This hybrid paper centrally corrects/reanalyzes the original New Haven data and re-runs Imai’s analyses, so reproduction is selected. It additionally reports new 2002 Iowa/Michigan experiments, confirming Gerber and Green (2000) and rejecting Imai’s large positive effect; new-sample evidence is kept out of reproduction axes. References to Gerber and Green (2001) and Green and Gerber (2001) supply contextual evidence, not distinct reanalyzed originals. No target DOI is printed in the reference list.
